title: Ultra-processed diets cause excess calorie intake and weight gain: an inpatient randomized controlled trial of ad libitum food intake
authors: Hall KD, Ayuketah A, Brychta R, Cai H, Cassimatis T, Chen KY, et al.
followUp: 14 days on each diet, 28 days as inpatients, crossover without washout
population: Weight-stable adults, 10 men and 10 women, aged 31.2 ± 1.6 years (mean ± SE), BMI 27 ± 1.5 kg/m2, at the NIH Clinical Center
funder: This work was supported by the Intramural Research Program of the National Institutes of Health, National Institute of Diabetes & Digestive & Kidney Diseases.
authorConflicts: CG Forde has received reimbursement for speaking at conferences sponsored by companies selling nutritional products, serves on the scientific advisory council for Kerry Taste and Nutrition, and is part of an academic consortium that has received research funding from Abbott Nutrition, Nestec and Danone. The other authors declared no conflicts.
result: Meals matched for presented energy, energy density including beverages, macronutrients, sugars, sodium and fibre; non-beverage energy density 1.957 kcal/g (ultra-processed) versus 1.057 kcal/g (unprocessed). Ad libitum energy intake 508 ± 106 kcal/day higher on the ultra-processed diet (carbohydrate 280 ± 54, fat 230 ± 53, protein −2 ± 12 kcal/day); weight +0.9 ± 0.3 kg versus −0.9 ± 0.3 kg; body fat +0.4 ± 0.1 kg versus −0.3 ± 0.1 kg; eating rate 17 ± 1 kcal/min and 7.4 ± 0.9 g/min faster; fibre intake 48.5 versus 45.8 g/day (P = 0.41); insoluble share of presented fibre about 16% versus 77%. Fasting PYY 25.1 versus 34.3 pg/ml (baseline 28.9); active ghrelin 54.1 versus 48.3 pg/ml (baseline 61.4). Mean ± SE. A 2019 erratum corrected meal-specific intakes; a 2020 erratum was not read.
